Execute a scope management plan to thoroughly understand the project scope and any dependencies within the project plan.

questions.solutionLine: A. Organize a project schedule network diagram to graphically represent the dependencies that exist between project schedule activities.
questions.explanation:
A project schedule network diagram is a graphical representation of the logical relationships, or dependencies, that exist between the project schedule activities. By having a clear understanding of which areas of the project are impacted by one another, the project manager can better prioritize any necessary adjustments to minimize the negative impact of a delay or change order on other areas of the project plan and schedule.

The other options are less effective.

The work breakdown structure and scope breakdown plan are both key documents that are used to inform the project management plan and project schedule, but they do not inherently map out the dependencies that exist between project schedule activities.

A product backlog is a useful approach in adaptive environments that allows the project team to dynamically adjust the workload to prioritize work items as needed, but the project manager must already have an understanding of the dependencies that exist between project schedule activities in order to minimize the negative impact of delays and adjustments.

questions.stem:
A manufacturing plant is planning a plant shutdown and turnaround. The project scope has a set baseline with minimal variation expected. Integration requirements are limited to ensuring compatibility with existing components. The sponsor instructs the project manager to outsource labor to a vendor specializing in minor turnarounds.

What should the project manager do?

options.text: Select a cost-plus-fixed-fee contract in which the vendor reimburses costs and pays negotiated professional service fees.
Negotiate a cost-plus-award-fee agreement to reward early delivery and incentivize contractor performance.
Offer a time and materials (T&M) contract option where costs are billed based on actual labor hours and purchased materials.
Choose a firm fixed-price contract to ensure cost predictability and transfer scope-related vendor risk responsibility.

questions.solutionLine: D. Choose a firm fixed-price contract to ensure cost predictability and transfer scope-related vendor risk responsibility.
questions.explanation:
The project manager should select a fixed-price contract when the scope is baselined and predictable, ensuring cost certainty and shifting risk to the seller. Fixed-price contracts are agreements that establish a predetermined fee for a clearly defined scope of work, transferring cost risk to the seller while offering budget predictability for the buyer.

The other options are incorrect.

A cost-plus-fixed-fee contract leaves most financial risk with the buyer, which is not needed when scope is stable.

A cost-plus-award-fee agreement is used when accelerated delivery or superior performance must be incentivized, which is not the case in this scenario.

A time and materials contract is best when scope is undefined or variable, which is not the case in this scenario.

questions.stem:
Before a daily coordination meeting, a scrum master runs some numbers that generate a burndown chart showing that the rate of work completed is slowing down. When the product owner sees the chart, they request that the scrum master identify what is blocking the project's progress.

What should the scrum master do in this scenario?

options.text: Encourage project team members to discuss any issues that might be slowing down project progress.
Coach project stakeholders on problem-solving techniques to help identify the source of the slowdown.
Explain that the team will monitor progress to ensure that impediments are resolved and will not recur.
Create a project interdependency profile, map, and timeline to visualize and track progress over time.

questions.solutionLine: A. Encourage project team members to discuss any issues that might be slowing down project progress.
questions.explanation:
The scrum master should encourage team members to discuss any issues that might be slowing progress. Because the chart was just recently generated, the scrum master has not yet had a chance to investigate the reasons it shows the results it shows.

The other options are incorrect.

The product owner asked the scrum master to identify the impediment. Coaching stakeholders on problem-solving techniques does not help identify or resolve the issue at hand.

Monitoring progress does not identify the source of the impediment.

Creating a project interdependency profile helps visualize and track interdependencies over time, but it does not identify and resolve the current blockers affecting project progress.

questions.stem:
In the planning phase of a development project, the team is discussing the proposed project scope. There is disagreement about the features that should be included. The project management office reminds the team that time and cost must be weighed against marketability, and that obtaining agreement from all stakeholders will be a challenge.

What should the project manager do?

options.text: Use diplomacy to smooth over the disagreements and press for a compromise solution that could win support.
Make a unilateral decision based on the evidence and allow the stakeholders time to discuss and reach an agreement.
Work directly with stakeholders to assess their competing ideas until they reach a consensus that meets the desired objectives.
Draft a first version of the project management plan to show how the preferred scope would look if accepted.

questions.solutionLine: C. Work directly with stakeholders to assess their competing ideas until they reach a consensus that meets the desired objectives.
questions.explanation:
The ability to confront disagreements directly exemplifies strong leadership, which is vital to being a good project manager. By working with stakeholders to assess the strengths and weaknesses of their competing ideas, the project manager has the best chance of persuading them to reach consensus.

The other options are incorrect.

Handling disagreements diplomatically and respectfully is always helpful. However, trying to smooth over and ignore disagreements is less likely to succeed than facing and working through them.

At some point, the project manager might have to make a unilateral decision based on the evidence. However, the first move should always be to hear from all stakeholders and work with them to resolve their different opinions.

By drafting a trial project management plan, the project manager might be able to present a fuller and more persuasive vision of the preferred solution. However, presenting a plan that failed to convince stakeholders would be a wasted effort.

questions.stem:
An e-commerce startup company is preparing to launch a large, wide-ranging project. A key stakeholder has raised concerns that the design team is pursuing ideas beyond what the available budget and realistic schedule can support. At the same time, the customer is encouraging the designers to think broadly and creatively. The sponsor directs the project manager to establish clear limits so the team knows exactly what is included in the project and what is not.

What should the project manager do?

options.text: Build a project profile matrix to estimate the overall effort required.
Develop a scope baseline that defines boundaries and deliverables.
Meet with the customer to discuss a realistic budget and timeline.
Share a mockup showing how the design supports the customer's vision.

questions.solutionLine: B. Develop a scope baseline that defines boundaries and deliverables.
questions.explanation:
The project manager should create a scope baseline to define the boundaries of the project. The scope baseline defines inclusions/exclusions, the work breakdown structure (WBS), and the WBS dictionary.

The other options are incorrect.

A detailed project profile matrix summarizes various aspects of a project and helps visualize relationships and prioritize tasks. It is an effort estimation tool; it is not the way to set project boundaries.

Meeting with the customer to explain what is possible is a good idea, but it would probably lead to a compromise rather than setting limits.

Sharing the design with the stakeholder will not lead to an increased budget or timeline needed to complete the project successfully. It helps visualization, but would not define project scope.

questions.stem:
A healthcare analytics provider is enhancing its patient insights platform to meet new data-sharing regulations. The project manager has completed scope evaluation, stakeholder alignment, and backlog reprioritization. A formal scope change has been approved and implemented. The team now needs to document how scope decisions connect to business and compliance drivers.

What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Retire the previous roadmap and initiate a new charter that is aligned with regulatory goals.
Expand the backlog to add additional features that support long-term analytics goals.
Submit the revised backlog to governance for final sign-off and funding allocation.
Use a traceability matrix to link updated scope items to business and compliance drivers.

questions.solutionLine: D. Use a traceability matrix to link updated scope items to business and compliance drivers.
questions.explanation:
The project manager should use traceability matrices to document how scope decisions align with business needs and external drivers. This supports auditability, stakeholder transparency, and future change control.

The other options are incorrect.

Retiring the roadmap and restarting the charter risks losing continuity and stakeholder buy-in.

Expanding scope again without evaluation risks misalignment.

Governance input is appropriate earlier in the process.

questions.stem:
A team is working in a highly regulated industry, and the compliance department keeps pushing documentation and process steps that interfere with the team’s desired way of working. The team is becoming increasingly frustrated with the compliance department, and they ask the project manager to intervene.

What should the project manager do?

options.text: Help the team understand that compliance is a crucial component of the project's overall success and value creation.
Push back on the compliance department and reduce the number of documents so the team can focus on value creation.
Conduct a daily workshop to assess compliance and complete as much compliance work as possible within that timebox.
Invite the compliance team to attend the daily coordination meetings to avoid interference and resentment between the two teams.

questions.solutionLine: A. Help the team understand that compliance is a crucial component of the project's overall success and value creation.
questions.explanation:
The compliance department is responsible for ensuring adherence to the defined project standards, rules, and procedures, as well as conducting project audits. By focusing on understanding and collaboration, the project manager can effectively address the team's concerns, maintain compliance with regulations, and ensure the project's overall success. This approach demonstrates a commitment to both project goals and regulatory compliance, fostering a more harmonious and productive working environment.

The other options are incorrect.

While the project manager may need to negotiate with the compliance department to streamline certain processes, simply pushing back and reducing documentation is not an appropriate solution. The team still needs to comply with all applicable regulations, and reducing documentation could increase the risk of non-compliance

While dedicating time to compliance is important, making it a daily focus could further disrupt the team's workflow and increase their frustration. The project manager should aim to integrate compliance activities into the team's regular processes rather than creating separate workshops.

While involving the compliance team in daily coordination meetings could foster transparency and communication, it may not be the most efficient use of everyone's time. The project manager should consider more targeted meetings or communication channels to address specific compliance concerns.

questions.stem:
A project manager is leading a global team in developing a new product for worldwide sale. The team consists of members from three continents. During a critical phase of the project, a misunderstanding stemming from differences in communication styles arises that threatens to derail progress.

What should the project manager do to resolve the friction?

options.text: Engage an expert to review the communications management plan and facilitate a discussion to improve communication dynamics and cultural awareness.
Hire a translation expert who can reframe each team’s language and word choices in a manner that is understandable to everyone on all three teams.
Request that a stakeholder mediate between the teams to ensure effective communication throughout the project's life cycle.
Involve a member of each team in decision-making processes to help reinforce ownership and commitment to project goals.

questions.solutionLine: A. Engage an expert to review the communications management plan and facilitate a discussion to improve communication dynamics and cultural awareness.
questions.explanation:
An expert can provide insights into cultural nuances, helping the team develop awareness and practices to respect and embrace diversity. Without a strong understanding of cultural differences, misunderstandings, misinterpretations, or conflicts can arise. An expert can evaluate the current communication dynamics, identify weaknesses, and recommend strategies to enhance clarity, inclusiveness, and effectiveness. When team members feel understood and that their cultural identity is valued, engagement and morale improve.

The other options are incorrect.

An interpreter would provide a literal translation of what an individual is saying, but that would not clarify the reasons for a team member’s silence or frustrations, for example.

It is not a stakeholder’s responsibility to mediate among teams when cultural issues arise.

Involving team members in making decisions is a good idea, but it does not address cultural differences or tensions.

questions.stem:
A product owner is leading an adaptive initiative to deliver a new mobile banking app. Stakeholders are brainstorming user stories, and the project team is beginning to discuss how many of them could fit into the next sprint. A developer asks how the team will know which stories are ready and prioritized for selection.

What should the Scrum team do?

options.text: Estimate the user stories using planning poker prioritization to establish team velocity.
Build a release roadmap to sequence the highest features across multiple iterations.
Define readiness criteria and prioritize the product backlog before the next sprint.
Break down the selected stories into tasks, and prioritize and order them for execution.

questions.solutionLine: C. Define readiness criteria and prioritize the product backlog before the next sprint.
questions.explanation:
The Scrum team must ensure the product backlog is refined, prioritized, and meets readiness criteria before the team can select items for the sprint backlog. This is the adaptive equivalent of scope planning.

The other options are incorrect.

Estimating without readiness is premature. Velocity estimates are unreliable if stories are not yet refined and prioritized.

Building a roadmap guides long-term sequencing. It is useful, but it does not solve the immediate readiness gap for sprint planning.

Task breakdown is scheduling, not scope planning, so this is a premature action. Breaking down and ordering tasks happens after the scope is set for the next sprint.

questions.stem:
A project team conducted a retrospective to identify lessons learned on a recent project. The results have been recorded in the lessons learned registry. The project manager is determined to not let these lessons be overlooked but to apply them to future work done by this project team.

What should the project manager do?

options.text: Use pictures and video to document the lessons learned more effectively.
Enter the lessons learned into the permanent lessons learned repository.
Use checklists to help identify similarities among the situations documented.
Use storytelling to make the lessons learned more relatable and memorable.

questions.solutionLine: D. Use storytelling to make the lessons learned more relatable and memorable.
questions.explanation:
The value of storytelling in project management is that narrative is a powerful tool for conveying lessons learned, good practices, and project outcomes. Information recorded in reports is easy to overlook, but storytelling engages the team and makes the lessons more memorable.

The other options are incorrect.

Knowledge can be documented by using any suitable means that ensures the efficiency of the lessons captured. Although pictures and video might be effective in some cases, text might be appropriate in many others.

Adding the information to the permanent lessons learned repository is a standard task at the end of the project. That makes the lessons learned available to others for future projects, but it does not support the manager’s goal of making sure the lessons learned are applied to the current project.

Checklists can be a helpful tool for identifying similarities among the situations documented during a project or across projects. However, checklists alone are not likely to help drive the team’s awareness in the way storytelling can.

questions.stem:
A junior project manager asks a senior colleague for help initiating the project closeout phase. During the discussion, the senior project manager notices that some client-requested changes are not clearly documented, and a few stakeholders have not confirmed whether the deliverables meet their expectations. The team is eager to finalize the project, but the senior project manager is concerned that premature closure could lead to issues post-implementation.

What should the senior project manager do first?

options.text: Review the change log and confirm all requested modifications were formally approved and implemented.
Validate that the customer has officially accepted the final project deliverables in writing.
Request feedback from remaining stakeholders to understand any concerns before closing the project.
Verify whether the final budget report and lessons learned register have been completed and archived.

questions.solutionLine: A. Review the change log and confirm all requested modifications were formally approved and implemented.
questions.explanation:
Before initiating project closeout, the senior project manager must confirm that all approved changes have been properly handled. Reviewing the change log helps ensure nothing was missed or left unresolved, which could otherwise undermine client satisfaction or lead to disputes.

The other options are incorrect.

Customer acceptance is essential, but if requested changes haven’t been tracked or implemented, any acceptance could be based on incomplete or inaccurate expectations.

Gathering feedback is useful, but the immediate priority is to verify formal change handling. Unaddressed change requests are a more critical risk.

Administrative closeout tasks like final budget and lessons learned are important, but they do not address the potential delivery gap identified.

questions.stem:
A small company has been acquired by a larger company. A project manager has been tasked with leading the marketing teams through the process of dealing with the organizational change resulting from the acquisition.

What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Arrange a meeting to introduce stakeholders to the teams, fostering understanding and communication.
Survey stakeholders from both companies and share their experiences with organizational change.
Review each company’s knowledge repositories to understand their different marketing approaches.
Identify the nature and scope of change, whether it is a shift in strategy, new leadership, or policy change.

questions.solutionLine: D. Identify the nature and scope of change, whether it is a shift in strategy, new leadership, or policy change.
questions.explanation:
The project manager should begin by clearly identifying the organizational change, whether it is a shift in strategy, restructuring, new leadership, or changes in policies. Understanding the nature and scope of the change is essential for assessing its impact.

The other options are incorrect.

Although it would be helpful if leadership were introduced to the teams, it is rare for leadership to have the time to be hands-on with the teams and the specifics of the process.

Sharing key stakeholders’ experiences with organizational change would not help the marketing team navigate the change process. This could be considered a supplementary enrichment action.

Reviewing knowledge repositories would help teams understand different marketing approaches, but it would not address organizational change. Before focusing on repositories or specific marketing approaches, the project manager must thoroughly understand the nature and scope of the change to effectively manage its implications.

questions.stem:
Two stakeholders disagree on whether to allocate additional resources to shorten the critical path tasks. The project sponsor argues for acceleration to potentially increase value. The engineering team states that additional resources will not reduce duration.

What should the project manager do?

options.text: Approve additional resources immediately to shorten the time needed to complete the project.
Reassess the critical path and discuss the findings with stakeholders before making a decision.
Facilitate a meeting between the stakeholders to discuss why more resources will not reduce duration.
Perform a Monte Carlo analysis to see how adding more resources can compress the project timeline.

questions.solutionLine: B. Reassess the critical path and discuss the findings with stakeholders before making a decision.
questions.explanation:
The project manager should perform a formal reassessment of the critical path and explain the results to the stakeholders before deciding on resource use. Reassessing the critical path and discussing the findings with stakeholders supports informed decision-making, risk mitigation, and alignment with project objectives.

The other options are less effective.

As the engineering lead pointed out, simply adding resources does not guarantee a shorter duration.

A meeting alone between the two stakeholders would not address the problem with achieving a shorter critical path.

Even though performing a Monte Carlo analysis would aid the quantitative aspect of the project, it would not necessarily address the additional resources needed to shorten the critical path.

questions.stem:
A project team piloted a new onboarding guide for external contractors, reducing ramp-up time by 30%. The guide was effective during the project, but is not yet part of the organization’s standard resources. The project manager must ensure this improvement is integrated into future projects.

What should the project manager do?

options.text: Capture the onboarding guide in the lessons learned register for use in future projects.
Share the onboarding guide informally with other project managers across the organization.
Ask the project sponsor to approve the onboarding guide for organizational use in future initiatives.
Request that the project management office (PMO) update the onboarding guide in the repository.

questions.solutionLine: D. Request that the project management office (PMO) update the onboarding guide in the repository.
questions.explanation:
Updating the onboarding guide institutionalizes the improvement and makes it reusable across projects. This ensures that the improvement becomes part of the organization’s standard resources and benefits future projects.

The other options are incorrect.

Lessons learned help awareness, but do not update process assets. Without updating organizational resources, the guide will still not become part of the organization’s standard resources.

Informal sharing spreads knowledge but does not institutionalize it.

Sponsor approval alone does not update process assets.

All of these options are helpful, but they are not enough to ensure the onboarding guide is standardized, reviewed, and consistently maintained at an organizational level.

questions.stem:
An energy infrastructure company is executing a series of initiatives to modernize its operations and align with strategic goals. A project manager has completed a change impact gap analysis and documented how strategic initiatives will affect systems and personnel. Management is aligned, but members of the research staff continue to raise the same issues, indicating that resistance needs to be addressed across departments.

What should the project manager do next?

options.text: Assemble a stakeholder directory to support the needed engagement efforts.
Assess the corporate culture to identify values and behaviors that influence opinions.
Summarize completed change analysis actions in a change log for internal review.
Schedule orientation sessions to introduce staff to the new strategic direction.

questions.solutionLine: B. Assess the corporate culture to identify values and behaviors that influence opinions.
questions.explanation:
Resistance often stems from deeper cultural factors, such as values, attitudes toward change, risk tolerance, or trust in leadership. Assessing corporate culture helps uncover how these factors shape the staff's opinions and concerns about the initiatives. A cultural assessment reveals underlying resistance factors and informs targeted interventions.

The other options are incorrect.

Building a stakeholder directory is useful for preparing for engagement, but it does not address cultural resistance.

Summarizing past change analysis actions taken does not advance the change process.

Orientation is premature without identifying the resistance drivers. By understanding the factors driving resistance, the project manager can tailor communication, onboarding, and engagement efforts to align with the company's values.

questions.stem:
A project manager has been hired to execute a plant turnaround. As the project progresses, the sponsor pressures the project manager to complete the turnaround two weeks earlier than planned without changing the scope. The engineering team lead warns that this timeline is not possible.

What should the project manager do?

options.text: Perform an impact analysis and submit a formal change request to revise the schedule.
Continue with the original schedule and arrange a meeting between the engineering lead and the project sponsor.
Submit a request for an increase in the budget to cover the cost of re-baselining the project schedule.
Remind the sponsor that full staffing cannot be in place two weeks early without additional pay.

questions.solutionLine: A. Perform an impact analysis and submit a formal change request to revise the schedule.
questions.explanation:
The project manager should perform an impact analysis and submit a change request for revising the schedule. This action ensures that any proposed changes to the project timeline are carefully evaluated for their effects on scope, cost, resources, and risks.

The other options are less effective.

Continuing with the original schedule ignores the pressure it places on the project, which in turn undermines credibility. A meeting between the two stakeholders could lead to a compromise, which would still require an impact analysis and a change control request for re-baselining.

Re-baseling the schedule might require additional funding, but funding alone won't solve the issue with the schedule.

If the staff were told they have a certain amount of time before the plant reopens, they might be unavailable to return two weeks early.

questions.stem:
A multinational home electronics manufacturer is updating its most popular appliance to strengthen global market share. During planning, marketing stakeholders push for the rapid release of the update to capture competitors’ sales. The operations manager warns that the existing product vision might no longer align with evolving customer expectations and regulatory requirements. The sponsor stresses that the project must adapt to remain strategically relevant and competitive across markets.

What should the project manager do? (Choose 2)

options.text: Perform a SWOT (strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats) analysis to identify factors affecting strategic market positioning.
Review historical sales performance trends to extrapolate insights for future market growth opportunities.
Prepare a market analysis report comparing competitors, risks, and potential expansion opportunities.
Incorporate insight from customer feedback from online registration and warranty surveys to refine product features and overall vision.
Facilitate revision of the organizational vision statement to realign long-term corporate strategic objectives.

questions.solutionLine: C, D
questions.explanation:
C. Prepare a market analysis report comparing competitors, risks, and potential expansion opportunities.

D. Incorporate insight from customer feedback from online registration and warranty surveys to refine product features and overall vision.

Preparing a market analysis report directly aligns with the sponsor's emphasis on ensuring the project remains relevant and competitive across markets. A market analysis provides insight into competitive positioning, emerging risks, and potential growth areas, enabling informed decision-making.

Customer feedback is essential to align the product vision with evolving customer expectations. Leveraging this data ensures the updated appliance meets actual user needs, strengthening global market appeal.

The other options are incorrect.

While a SWOT analysis is a valuable tool for strategic planning, it is more general and lacks the specificity needed to address competitive market updates or direct customer insights.

Historical sales data might indicate past performance, but it does not necessarily reflect the current or future market context, especially when customer preferences and regulatory conditions are evolving.

Rewriting organizational vision statements may not be necessary and is beyond the project manager's authority.

questions.stem:
A company is initiating a large project that must be delivered under strict budget, resource, and schedule limitations. Senior management has emphasized that any deviation from these constraints will not be acceptable because funding is tight and customer expectations are high. The sponsor directs the project manager to ensure that all required deliverables can be achieved within the approved timeline and budget, despite the restrictive conditions.

What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Work with stakeholders to set a scope baseline that defines boundaries and deliverables.
Prepare a communication plan to keep stakeholders engaged and aligned with the objectives.
Conduct a complexity assessment to estimate the overall project size and risk exposure.
Build a detailed profile matrix to calculate the effort to complete the major deliverables.

questions.solutionLine: A. Work with stakeholders to set a scope baseline that defines boundaries and deliverables.
questions.explanation:
The scope statement establishes project boundaries and measurable objectives within constraints.

The first step the project manager should take is working with stakeholders to set a scope baseline that defines project boundaries and deliverables. Clarifying deliverables and boundaries upfront helps the project manager set a clear basis for accurately estimating timelines, budgets, and resource needs.

The other options are incorrect.

A communications management plan supports engagement, but does not establish scope or boundaries.

Conducting a complexity assessment informs planning, but it does not define the project scope or what can be achieved within the approved timeline and budget, despite the restrictive conditions.

Effort estimates belong to detailed planning, not boundary definition.

questions.stem:
Upon completing the first quarter of the planned project duration, the project manager conducts a performance review and calculates the schedule variance (SV) as –$10,500. (All monetary figures are in US dollars.)

What does this indicate about the project's progress?

options.text: The project is ahead of schedule by $10,500 worth of work.
The project is behind schedule by $10,500 worth of work.
The project is on schedule, and everything is progressing smoothly.
The team will need to work overtime to catch up.

questions.solutionLine: B. The project is behind schedule by $10,500 worth of work.
questions.explanation:
The schedule variance (SV) is a measure of schedule performance expressed as the difference between the earned value (EV) and the planned value (PV).

Schedule variance (SV) is calculated as follows:

• SV = EV – PV

A negative SV (–$10,500) means the project has completed less work than planned at this stage, which indicates a schedule delay.

All other options are incorrect.

The project is not ahead of schedule by $10,500 worth of work because a negative SV indicates the project is behind schedule, not ahead. If the project were ahead, SV would be positive.

It is incorrect that the project is on schedule because if the project were exactly on schedule, SV would be zero.

Working overtime to catch up is not the best or only solution to address schedule delays. The project manager should first analyze the root cause of the delay before deciding on corrective actions.
